blocks.text: These learning questions turn Module 1 into an active-recall map of the cell. They move from evolutionary logic and cellular building blocks into membranes, organelles, energy conversion, the cytoskeleton, and the nucleus, so use them to practise connecting named structures to their biological jobs.
What this set is testing

items: Evolution and endosymbiosis questions test whether you can explain evidence, sequence, and domain-level differences rather than just list definitions.
Macromolecule, membrane, and endomembrane questions check structure-function logic: what a component is made of, where it sits, and what process it supports.
Respiration, photosynthesis, cytoskeleton, ECM, and nucleus questions reward process order, compartment names, and clear links between cellular organisation and function.

blocks.text: How to practise

For every answer, force yourself to include a location, a mechanism, and a consequence. If a question mentions an organelle or membrane, do not stop at naming it; explain what that structure enables and why the cell needs it.
1. Evolution, Natural Selection, and Endosymbiosis (Lecture 1)

Modes of Selection: Identify the three modes of selection (Directional, Disruptive, Stabilising) shown in mice population graphs, and determine which type applies when predators target specific fur colours (2023, Q5).
Evidence for Endosymbiosis: State two common features shared by mitochondria and chloroplasts that support the theory that they were once independent bacteria (2024, Q2b).
2. Building Blocks and Metabolism (Lecture 2)
Metabolic Concepts: Outline the specific difference between catabolism and anabolism with respect to energy (2023, Q9b).
3. The Plasma Membrane (Lecture 3)
Membrane Characteristics: Identify the plasma membrane as a specific type of "barrier" (semi-permeable) that surrounds cells and organelles (2021, Q1-i).
4. Endomembrane System and Bulk Transport (Lecture 4)
The Golgi Complex: Outline one key function of the Golgi complex (2022, Q1c).
Vesicle Tagging: Describe the purpose of "tagging" vesicles that leave the Golgi complex (Lecture 4 Practice Question).
Mechanism of Secretion: Identify that Extracellular Matrix (ECM) proteins are released from the cell via the process of constitutive exocytosis (2022, Q1b; 2025, Q1b).
Synthesis Location: Identify the Rough ER as the site where ECM proteins are synthesised (2025, Q1b).

chapters.title: 5. Cytoskeleton, Cell Junctions, and the ECM (Lecture 5)

blocks.text: 5. Cytoskeleton, Cell Junctions, and the ECM (Lecture 5)
Cytoskeletal Components:

Identify the proteins that make up microfilaments (actin) and their role in resisting tension (2024, Q1a). Identify the role of intermediate filaments in forming nuclear structures like the lamina (2024, Q1a). Provide examples of microtubules' involvement in cell motility, such as flagella (2024, Q1b).
Cell Junctions:
Identify and distinguish between Tight Junctions, Desmosomes, and Gap Junctions based on their functions, such as preventing fluid movement or allowing rapid communication (2022, Q1a; 2024, Q1c).
ECM Components:

Match letters from a diagram to descriptions of ECM components, including those that trap water (proteoglycans), resist tension (collagen), and attach cells to the matrix (fibronectin/integrins) (2025, Q1a). Identify integrins as the proteins connecting the ECM to the internal cytoskeleton (2022, Q1b).
Intracellular Movement: Identify that vesicles move along microtubules using motor proteins (2022, Q1b).
6. Cellular Respiration and Photosynthesis (Lectures 6 & 7)
Respiration Process:

Identify the mitochondrion as the site of respiration and the intermembrane space as the area of highest proton concentration (2022, Q2a; 2024, Q2a). Identify which specific steps of respiration occur in the mitochondrial matrix (2022, Q2b). Complete a process flow describing the respiratory electron transport chain, protons, ATP synthase, and the generation of ATP (2024, Q2a).
Photosynthesis Process:

Identify the chloroplast as the site of photosynthesis and the thylakoid space as the area of highest proton concentration (2022, Q2a). Explain how the absence of light affects photosynthetic electron transport, the proton gradient, and ATP production (2023, Q2b).
Shared Mechanisms:

Name the protein complex essential for both respiration and photosynthesis (ATP synthase) and label the membrane/compartments used by both (2023, Q2a). Contrast the usage of ATP produced in respiration (cellular work) versus photosynthesis (used in the Calvin Cycle) (2022, Q2a).
7. The Nucleus (Lecture 9)
Nuclear Structure:

Label parts of the nucleus in an electron micrograph, including the nucleolus and chromatin (2019, Q1). Identify the nuclear envelope as being formed from two membranes and its continuity with the endoplasmic reticulum (2021, Q1-ii). Name the nuclear lamina as the structure lining the inner surface of the envelope and identify its cytoskeletal composition (intermediate filaments) (2024, Q1a; 2023, Q2d).

chapters.title: Part 1 - Evolution, Natural Selection, and Endosymbiosis

blocks.text: Part 1 - Evolution, Natural Selection, and Endosymbiosis
1. Natural Selection and Modes of Evolution

Requirements for Natural Selection: To correctly answer what is required for natural selection to act as a mechanism for evolution, you must list four specific conditions: Variation (individuals in a population must vary from one another), Inheritance (parents must pass on their traits to offspring genetically), Selection (some variants must reproduce more than others), and Time (successful variations must accumulate over many generations).
Mechanisms of Selection: Evolution acts not only on physical shape or colour but also on biological molecules and DNA sequences.
Identifying Modes of Selection (Exam Application):
Directional Selection: Occurs when the population shifts toward one extreme phenotype.
Disruptive Selection: Occurs when both extremes are favoured over the intermediate; this happens if predators target individuals with the intermediate fur colour.
Stabilising Selection: Occurs when the intermediate phenotype is favoured; for example, if predators target mice with white or black fur (the extremes), the population stabilises in the middle.

Continuous Variation: When asked what explains the continuous range of a trait (like colour) in a species, you should state that it is driven by genetic variation in addition to environmental factors.
2. The Endosymbiosis Theory
Core Definition: This theory states that two key organelles in eukaryotes-mitochondria and chloroplasts-are derived from independent bacteria that were engulfed and "tamed" by ancestral eukaryotes.
Specific Ancestors: You must specify that mitochondria are derived from proteobacteria, while chloroplasts are derived from cyanobacteria.
The Evolutionary Sequence: Endosymbiosis happened twice: first for mitochondria, and then later for chloroplasts.
Providing Evidence (1-Mark/2-Mark Questions): When asked for features that support this theory, state that both organelles:

Contain their own DNA and ribosomes. Are able to make some of their own proteins independently of the nucleus. Are surrounded by multiple membranes (an outer and inner membrane, with chloroplasts having a third internal thylakoid system).
3. The Tree of Life and Phylogenetics
Defining a Phylogenetic Tree: These trees represent the relationships and family history of organisms built by identifying shared characters.
Types of Characters: Characters used for these trees can be physical traits or sequence information from biological molecules (DNA/RNA).
The Three Domains: All life is organised into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukaryotes.
Domain Characteristics:

Bacteria uniquely contain peptidoglycan in their cell walls and have circular chromosomes. Archaea also have circular chromosomes but lack peptidoglycan; some species can grow at temperatures exceeding 100°C. Eukaryotes are defined by the presence of a nuclear envelope and membrane-enclosed organelles.
4. LUCA (Last Universal Common Ancestor)
Age and Origin: LUCA is estimated to have lived approximately 4.0 to 4.3 billion years ago.
Reconstructing LUCA: We learn about LUCA's biology by identifying traits and molecules that are shared by all life currently on Earth.
LUCA's Features: Reconstructions suggest LUCA possessed an ancestral phospholipid cell membrane, used ATP synthase for energy, and had an early immune system.
5. Scale of Life

Relative Sizes: For questions requiring you to arrange structures by size, the general descending order is: Chicken egg (largest) > Human egg > Animal cell > Nucleus > Mitochondrion > Small bacterial cell > Virus > Ribosome > Protein (smallest).
Biological Breadth: The scale of life on Earth is vast, stretching from nanometers (molecules) to kilometers (ecosystems/biosphere).
Part 2 - Building Blocks and Metabolism
1. Structural Hierarchy and Scale
The Bottom-Up Approach: You must be able to describe how cells are organised from simple units into complex systems.
Building Blocks (Monomers): Amino acids, nucleobases, simple carbohydrates (monosaccharides), glycerol, and fatty acids.
Macromolecules (Polymers): These are created by joining building blocks with strong covalent bonds. Examples include proteins, DNA/RNA, and complex carbohydrates.
Supramolecular Assemblies: Large structures formed from macromolecules, such as membranes, ribosomes, and chromatin.
Scale of Life: Remember that a mammalian cell is approximately 70% water. Proteins are the most abundant organic component (~18%), followed by lipids (~5%) and nucleic acids (~1.35%).
2. Carbohydrates (Energy and Structure)
Monosaccharides (The Units):
Hexoses (e.g., Glucose) are the primary building blocks for energy and higher-order structures. Pentoses (e.g., Ribose, Deoxyribose) are specific 5-carbon sugars used in nucleic acids.
Polysaccharides (The Chains):
Energy Storage: Plants use starch (amylose/amylopectin); animals use glycogen. Both are polymers of glucose.
Structure: Cellulose is the primary structural component of plant cell walls and is a major source of dietary fibre.
Recognition: Carbohydrates on the cell surface function in cell-cell recognition and can be docking sites for viruses or toxins.
3. Lipids (Non-Polymeric and Hydrophobic)
Key Distinction: Unlike proteins or carbohydrates, lipids are non-polymeric. They do not form long chains of repeating identical units.
Structural Roles: Phospholipids and cholesterol are essential for membrane structure. Phospholipids are amphipathic, meaning they have a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails.
Regulatory Roles: Steroids (like cholesterol) act as precursors for vital hormones, such as testosterone and estradiol.
Energy Role: Triacylglycerols (TAG) provide high-density, long-term energy storage.
4. Proteins (The Cellular Workhorses)
Building Block: Proteins are polymers of amino acids. There are 20 different amino acids, each distinguished by its unique 'R' group (side chain), which determines its chemical properties.
Synthesis Path: Genetic information flows from DNA → mRNA → Protein. Proteins are assembled on ribosomes.
Diverse Functions: You must be able to list specific examples, such as catalytic (enzymes), structural (collagen), transport (haemoglobin), and regulatory (insulin).
5. Nucleic Acids (Information Carriers)
Building Block: The nucleotide, consisting of a phosphate group, a sugar, and a nitrogenous base.
DNA vs. RNA (Common Exam Distinctions):
Sugar: DNA uses deoxyribose (lacks an oxygen at the 2' position); RNA uses ribose.
Bases: DNA uses Thymine (T); RNA uses Uracil (U).
Structure: DNA is typically a double helix; RNA is usually single-stranded but folds into specific 3D shapes.
6. Metabolism: Catabolism vs. Anabolism
Exam questions (e.g., 2023, Q9b) frequently ask for the energy-based difference between these two pathways:
Catabolism: The process of breaking down complex molecules (like glucose) into simpler ones. This is an exergonic process that releases energy, which the cell captures as ATP.
Anabolism: The process of building complex molecules (making new materials). This is an endergonic process that requires an input of energy (ATP).
The ATP Link: Catabolism provides the energy needed to drive anabolic reactions, creating a continuous cycle of energy transfer.
Part 3 - The Plasma Membrane
1. The Plasma Membrane as a Barrier
Defining the Barrier (2021 Exam Application): When asked to identify the nature of the plasma membrane, you must define it as a semi-permeable barrier.

Permeability Logic: To answer questions about what can cross the membrane independently, remember the "lipid-soluble" rule. Hydrophobic/lipid-soluble molecules (such as steroid hormones and gases like $O_2$ and $CO_2$) can move directly through the bilayer via diffusion.
Restricted Substances: Large, polar, or charged molecules (like glucose and ions) are restricted and require specific membrane proteins to cross.
2. Membrane Fluidity and Regulation
Exam questions often focus on how a cell maintains the "fluid" state of its membrane under varying conditions:
Fatty Acid Saturation: Unsaturated tails have kinks that prevent tight packing, keeping the membrane fluid. Saturated tails pack tightly, making the membrane more viscous.
The Role of Cholesterol: This is a frequent target for "Explain" questions. Cholesterol acts as a fluidity buffer:
At moderate temperatures, it reduces fluidity by hindering phospholipid movement. At low temperatures, it disrupts the tight packing of tails, preventing the membrane from solidifying.
3. Diversity of Membrane Protein Functions
You should be prepared to list and explain the six primary roles of membrane proteins:
Signal Transduction: Relaying external chemical messages (like hormones) into the cell.
Cell-Cell Recognition: Using glycoproteins (proteins with carbohydrate tags) as identification markers.
Intercellular Joining: Linking adjacent cells together.
Transport: Moving specific solutes across the barrier.
Linking to Cytoskeleton/ECM: Using proteins like integrins to provide structural stability between the cell's interior and the extracellular matrix.
Enzymatic Activity: Carrying out metabolic pathways on the membrane surface.
4. Transport Mechanisms (Passive vs. Active)
For written or MCQ questions regarding movement, use this classification:
Passive Transport (No ATP):
Diffusion: Movement of lipid-soluble molecules down their concentration gradient.
Facilitated Diffusion: Movement of hydrophilic molecules down a gradient through channels (tunnels) or carriers (which change shape).
Osmosis: The diffusion of water through aquaporins.
Active Transport (Requires ATP):
Uses carrier proteins to move substances against their concentration gradient (from low to high). This is essential for maintaining internal concentrations, such as the sodium-potassium balance.
Co-transport (Indirect Active Transport):
A primary pump (using ATP) creates a gradient for one substance. The potential energy of that gradient is then used to power the transport of a second substance against its own gradient.
5. Importance of Organelles and Compartmentalisation
Questions regarding why eukaryotes have organelles should be answered using three core points:
Specialisation: They provide specialized environments for different processes (e.g., the acidic interior of a lysosome).
Efficiency: They allow incompatible reactions to occur simultaneously by keeping them separate.
Gradients: They enable the creation of concentration gradients (e.g., the proton gradient in mitochondria or chloroplasts), which are essential for energy production.

chapters.title: Part 4 - Endomembrane System and Bulk Transport

blocks.text: Part 4 - Endomembrane System and Bulk Transport
1. The Endomembrane System Overview

Definition: When asked to define this system, state that it is a collection of internal membranes in eukaryotic cells that are either physically continuous or connected via the transfer of membrane segments as vesicles.
Core Components: You must be able to list the following as members of the system: the nuclear envelope, endoplasmic reticulum (ER), Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, vacuoles, and the plasma membrane.
2. Functions of the Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)
Exam questions frequently require you to distinguish between the two distinct regions of the ER:

Rough ER (rER): Named for the ribosomes attached to its surface, it is the primary site for protein synthesis. This specifically includes proteins destined for secretion (like extracellular matrix proteins), insertion into membranes, or those to be wrapped within organelles.
Smooth ER (sER): Lacks ribosomes and performs diverse metabolic tasks. Key roles include:

Lipid synthesis (oils, phospholipids, and steroids). Metabolism of carbohydrates. Detoxification of drugs and poisons (particularly prominent in liver cells). Storage of calcium ions, which are released as triggers for cellular responses.
Dynamic Nature: It is important to note that the amount of sER in a cell is not fixed and can increase or decrease to meet specific metabolic demands.
3. The Golgi Complex: The Cell's Post Office
Primary Function: Describe its role as a "warehouse" that receives, modifies, sorts, and ships products arriving from the ER.

Polarity (Cis vs. Trans): You must correctly identify the direction of flow. The cis face is the receiving side (near the ER), and the trans face is the shipping side where vesicles pinch off to travel to other sites.
Modifications (Glycosylation): The Golgi modifies proteins by adding or altering carbohydrates (creating glycoproteins), which is vital for their final function.

The Purpose of Tagging: When asked why vesicles are "tagged" before leaving the Golgi, explain that molecular markers (like mannose-6-phosphate for lysosomal enzymes) are added to act like "zip codes," ensuring vesicles reach their correct delivery location, such as a specific organelle or the plasma membrane.
4. Bulk Transport Processes
Questions regarding how cells move large quantities of material across the plasma membrane use specific terminology:
Exocytosis (Moving OUT):
Constitutive Exocytosis: A continuous process used to release materials like extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins. It occurs in all cells and does not require an external signal.
Regulated Exocytosis: Materials (like hormones or neurotransmitters) are stored in vesicles and released only in response to a specific stimulus.
Endocytosis (Moving IN):
Phagocytosis: Often called "cell eating," where a cell engulfs large particles or whole organisms into a food vacuole.
Pinocytosis: Often called "cell drinking," this is the non-selective uptake of extracellular fluid and its dissolved solutes.
Receptor-mediated Endocytosis: A highly selective form of pinocytosis where specific molecules (ligands) bind to receptors on the membrane to trigger vesicle formation.
5. Lysosomes and Waste Management
Structure and Environment: Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs of hydrolytic enzymes. They maintain an acidic interior pH, which is the optimal environment for these enzymes to function.
Autophagy: This is a specific process where lysosomes use their enzymes to recycle the cell's own damaged or unwanted organelles and macromolecules.
6. Secretion Path Case Study (Exam Application)
Based on past exam questions (e.g., 2022 and 2025), you may be asked to trace the path of a secreted protein like collagen:
Synthesis: The protein is manufactured by ribosomes on the Rough ER.
Trafficking: It is sent to the cis face of the Golgi complex for processing and glycosylation.
Delivery: It is "tagged" and leaves the trans face of the Golgi in a vesicle.
Transport: The vesicle is moved through the cytoplasm by motor proteins that "walk" along microtubule tracks.
Release: The protein is released to the extracellular space via constitutive exocytosis.

chapters.title: Part 5 - Cytoskeleton, Cell Junctions, and the ECM

blocks.text: Part 5 - Cytoskeleton, Cell Junctions, and the ECM
1. The Cytoskeleton: Structure and Function
Exam questions often require you to identify the specific protein composition and mechanical role of the three major fiber types:
Microtubules:
Composition: Hollow tubes made of tubulin dimers.
Function: They resist compression and serve as "tracks" for motor proteins to transport vesicles.
Motility: They are the structural basis for cilia and flagella. In exams, use these as examples of microtubule-driven motility.
Microfilaments (Actin Filaments):
Composition: Two intertwined strands of actin.
Function: They are designed to resist tension.
Cortical Network: They form a network just under the plasma membrane to help maintain cell shape. They are also essential for muscle contraction.
Intermediate Filaments:
Composition: Fibrous proteins (like keratins or lamins) supercoiled into cables.
Function: They provide permanent structural support and anchor the nucleus and other organelles.
Nuclear Lamina: Specifically, intermediate filaments form the nuclear lamina that lines the inner surface of the nuclear envelope.
2. Cell Junctions: Linking Animal Cells
You must distinguish between the three types based on their primary biological task:
Tight Junctions: These form a continuous seal around cells to prevent the leakage of extracellular fluid across a layer of epithelial cells.

Desmosomes (Anchoring Junctions): These act like "rivets" to fasten cells together into strong sheets. They are physically connected to the cytoskeleton by intermediate filaments. A common exam application identifies "torn muscles" as effectively torn desmosomes.
Gap Junctions (Communicating Junctions): These provide cytoplasmic channels (similar to plant plasmodesmata) that allow for the rapid exchange of ions and small molecules between adjacent cells.
3. The Extracellular Matrix (ECM)
Origin and Secretion: The ECM is the non-cellular part of tissues. Its components are synthesised in the Rough ER and released via constitutive exocytosis (a continuous process).
Key Components (Diagram Matching):
Collagen: The most abundant glycoprotein; it provides high tensile strength and resists being pulled apart.
Proteoglycans: These consist of a small core protein with many carbohydrate chains; they are vital for trapping water to keep tissues hydrated and "plump".
Fibronectins: Glycoproteins that help attach the cell to the ECM.

The Bridge (Integrins): Integrins are the specific membrane proteins that span the plasma membrane to physically connect the ECM to the internal cytoskeleton. This allows for communication between a cell's exterior and interior environment.
4. Intracellular Movement (2022 Exam Application)
When asked how materials (like ECM proteins) are moved within the cell before secretion:

State that they are carried in vesicles. Specify that these vesicles travel along microtubule tracks. Identify that the movement is powered by motor proteins that "walk" the vesicles to their destination.
Part 6 - Cellular Respiration and Photosynthesis
1. Major Energy Requirements of the Cell
Exam questions often ask you to identify why a cell needs energy. You should list the four primary requirements:
Mechanical work: For example, the movement of motor proteins that "walk" vesicles along cytoskeletal tracks.
Making new materials: Synthesising macromolecules needed for growth and replacement.
Transport: Moving molecules across membranes against their concentration gradients.
Maintaining order: Ensuring the cell remains organised and functional.
2. Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) and the Energy Cycle
Structure: Composed of an adenine base, a ribose sugar, and a triphosphate group (three phosphate groups).

The Cycle: ATP is the primary energy carrier. Cells continuously regenerate ATP by using energy from catabolism to combine ADP and an inorganic phosphate ($P_i$). Hydrolysis of ATP then releases this stored energy for cellular work.
3. Cellular Respiration (Mitochondria)
Structure and Function: Mitochondria are the sites of respiration, with numbers ranging from 1 to 1000s per cell depending on energy demand. They contain their own DNA and ribosomes.
Respiration Equation: $C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O + \text{Energy}$.
The Three Stages:
Glycolysis: Occurs in the cytosol; breaks glucose into pyruvate.
Pyruvate Oxidation & Citric Acid Cycle: Occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. Pyruvate is converted to Acetyl CoA, releasing $CO_2$ and producing ATP, NADH, and $FADH_2$.

Oxidative Phosphorylation: Occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane. It consists of the Electron Transport Chain (ETC), which uses electrons from NADH and $FADH_2$ to pump protons into the intermembrane space, and Chemiosmosis, where protons flow through ATP synthase to generate the bulk of the cell's ATP.
Exam Note: The intermembrane space has the highest concentration of protons ($H^+$) during respiration.
4. Photosynthesis (Chloroplasts)
Equation: $6CO_2 + 6H_2O + \text{Light} \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2$.
The Two Stages:
Light Reactions: Occur on the thylakoid membrane. They capture light energy to split water (releasing $O_2$ as a byproduct) and produce ATP and NADPH.
The Calvin Cycle: Occurs in the stroma. It uses the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to fix $CO_2$ into sugar (glucose).
Calvin Cycle Detail: A 5-carbon compound (RuBP) is made during the Regeneration stage.
Exam Note: The thylakoid space has the highest concentration of protons during photosynthesis.
5. Comparative and Applied Concepts

Shared Mechanism: Both respiration and photosynthesis use an electron transport chain to establish a proton gradient across a membrane, which then powers the protein complex ATP synthase to manufacture ATP.

ATP Usage Difference: A common exam distinction is that ATP produced in respiration is used for general cellular work, whereas ATP produced in photosynthesis is used specifically within the Calvin Cycle for carbon fixation.

The Absence of Light: In exam application questions (e.g., 2023), if a plant is placed in the dark, the light reactions stop, the proton gradient in the thylakoid dissipates, and ATP synthesis via ATP synthase ceases.
Trophic Groups: Organisms like Paramecium that feed on organic matter are classified as consumers (heterotrophs), whereas plants are producers (autotrophs).
Part 7 - The Nucleus
1. Plant Cell Walls: Structure and Composition
Exam questions often focus on the chemical and functional differences between the two stages of the plant cell wall:
Primary Cell Wall:
Structure: A two-phase system consisting of crystalline cellulose microfibrils embedded in a non-crystalline matrix.
Matrix Components: Includes hemicellulose (rigid side chains) and pectin (negatively charged, traps water to form a gel).
Regulation: The protein extensin cross-links the components to control the wall's "extensibility" and limit cell expansion.
Secondary Cell Wall:
Timing: Produced only after cell growth has stopped.
Composition: Contains more cellulose and the complex polymer lignin.
Function: Lignin provides extreme rigidity and excludes water, making it essential for water-transporting cells (xylem).
2. Plant Shape and Turgor Pressure
You should be able to explain how plant cells maintain their structure without a skeleton:
The Vacuole: A large central organelle that contains high concentrations of solutes.
Osmosis: Water enters the vacuole via osmosis, causing the protoplast to expand and push against the rigid cell wall.
Turgor Pressure: This internal pressure makes the cell turgid, providing structural support for the whole plant.
Drought Application: If a plant is under drought stress, the vacuoles shrink due to water loss, the protoplast stops pushing against the wall, and the plant wilts.
3. Intercellular Communication (Plasmodesmata)
Structure: Continuous cytoplasmic channels that bridge the cell walls of adjacent plant cells.
Function: They allow for the free exchange of small molecules and water between cells.
Exam Application: When asked how viruses travel from one plant cell to another, identify the plasmodesmata as the specific structural route they exploit.
4. The Nucleus: Structure and Organisation
Exam questions frequently use electron micrographs and structural identification:
The Nuclear Envelope: A double membrane (two lipid bilayers). The outer membrane is continuous with the Endoplasmic Reticulum.
Nuclear Pores: Protein channels (nucleoporins) that strictly regulate exchange; they allow mRNA and ribosomal subunits OUT and bring control signals and energy IN.
The Nuclear Lamina: A network of intermediate filaments (specifically lamins) lining the inner surface of the envelope to maintain its shape.
DNA Packaging (Beads on a String): DNA wraps around histone proteins to form nucleosomes (10-nm fibre). These coil into 30-nm and 300-nm fibres before forming metaphase chromosomes for division.
5. Functional Chromatin and the Nucleolus
You must distinguish between the packed states of DNA:
Euchromatin: Loosely packed and containing active genes that the cell is currently using.
Heterochromatin: Densely packed and containing silent genes not in use.
The Nucleolus: A prominent, non-membrane-bound structure within the nucleus.
Function: It is the specific site where ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is synthesised and ribosomal subunits are assembled.

Micrograph Identification: In exam images, the nucleolus (A) is the dark, dense circular region, while the chromatin (B/C) consists of the lighter (eu-) or darker (hetero-) granular material filling the rest of the nucleus.
Worked answers
1. Nucleus Micrograph Identification (2019, Q1a)
Question: Label the three structures (A, B, C) and the surrounding structure (D) in the provided electron micrograph of a nucleus.
Thorough Answer:

A: Nucleolus. This is the dense, non-membrane-bound region responsible for ribosomal RNA (rRNA) synthesis and the assembly of ribosomal subunits. B: Heterochromatin. This is the densely packed, dark-staining chromatin containing genes that are currently silent or not in use by the cell. C: Euchromatin. This is the loosely packed, lighter-staining chromatin containing active genes being used for transcription. D: Nuclear Envelope. This is the double-membrane structure (two lipid bilayers) that encloses the nucleus.
2. Nucleo-Cytoplasmic Exchange (2019, Q1b)
Question: Name two types of molecules that exit and two that enter the nucleus via the nuclear pore.
Thorough Answer:
Molecules that EXIT: mRNA (carrying genetic instructions to ribosomes), tRNA, and ribosomal subunits manufactured in the nucleolus.
Molecules that ENTER: Control signals (to turn genes on or off), energy (in the form of ATP for synthesis), and building blocks for RNA synthesis.
3. Chromatin Structure and Function (2019, Q1c)
Question: Describe how euchromatin is both structurally AND functionally different from heterochromatin.

Thorough Answer: Structurally, euchromatin is less tightly packed and less electron-opaque, whereas heterochromatin is highly packed and more electron-opaque. Functionally, euchromatin contains active genes that the cell is currently using, while heterochromatin contains silent genes that are not being used.
4. Modes of Natural Selection (2023, Q5)
Question: Identify the type of selection shown in graphs where fur colour frequencies shift or split.
Thorough Answer:
Graph 1 (Directional Selection): The population shifts toward one extreme phenotype (e.g., only dark fur).
Graph 2 (Disruptive Selection): Both extremes are favoured over the intermediate phenotype; this occurs if predators specifically target the "middle" fur colour.
Graph 3 (Stabilising Selection): The intermediate phenotype is favoured, and extremes are selected against (e.g., if predators target both very light and very dark mice).
5. Metabolism: Catabolism vs. Anabolism (2023, Q9b)
Question: With respect to energy, outline the difference between catabolism and anabolism.

Thorough Answer: Catabolism is an exergonic process that involves the breakdown of complex organic molecules to release energy, which the cell captures as ATP. Anabolism is an endergonic process that involves the synthesis of complex materials (for growth/replacement) and requires an input of energy.
6. ATP Synthase Locations (2021, Q2c)
Question: In a plant cell, which organelles contain ATP synthase?

Thorough Answer: Both mitochondria and chloroplasts contain ATP synthase. In mitochondria, it is used during cellular respiration on the inner membrane, and in chloroplasts, it is used during the light reactions on the thylakoid membrane.
7. Exocytosis Varieties (2021, Q1c)
Question: Outline the difference between constitutive and regulated exocytosis and provide an example of each.

Thorough Answer: Constitutive exocytosis is a continuous process occurring in all cells to release materials like Extracellular Matrix (ECM) proteins. Regulated exocytosis occurs only in response to a specific external signal or stimulus; an example is the release of hormones (like insulin) or neurotransmitters.
8. Endosymbiosis Evidence (2024, Q2b)
Question: State two features common to mitochondria and chloroplasts that support the endosymbiont theory.

Thorough Answer: Both organelles contain their own DNA (circular chromosomes) and their own ribosomes, allowing them to synthesize some of their own proteins. Additionally, both are enclosed by multiple membranes, consistent with being engulfed by an ancestral cell.
9. Respiratory Organelle and Mechanism (2024, Q2a)
Question: Fill in the gaps regarding the site and mechanism of cellular respiration.

Thorough Answer: The mitochondrion is the organelle where respiration occurs. It has folds called cristae on the inner membrane. This membrane contains the respiratory electron transport chain that accepts electrons from NADH and $FADH_2$. This leads to an accumulation of protons in the intermembrane space, which then pass back into the matrix through ATP synthase to generate ATP.
10. Cytoskeletal Properties (2024, Q1a)
Question: Complete the sentences regarding microfilaments and intermediate filaments.
Thorough Answer: Microfilaments are made from actin proteins and are able to resist tension. Intermediate filaments form permanent structures such as the lamina in the nucleus.
11. Microtubules and Cell Motility (2024, Q1b)
Question: Provide two examples where microtubules are involved in motility.
Thorough Answer: Microtubules are the primary structural components powering the movement of flagella (snake-like motion) and cilia (rowing motion).
12. Animal Cell Junctions (2022, Q1a)
Question: Identify the functions of junctions X, Y, and Z.
Thorough Answer:
X (Tight Junction): Forms a seal to prevent fluid movement across cell layers.
Y (Desmosome): Acts as a rivet to fasten cells together into strong sheets; connected internally by intermediate filaments.
Z (Gap Junction): Provides cytoplasmic channels between adjacent cells for rapid communication of ions and small molecules.
13. ATP Usage Comparison (2022, Q2a)
Question: Contrast the usage of ATP produced in respiration versus photosynthesis.

Thorough Answer: ATP produced during cellular respiration is used to power general cellular work (mechanical, transport, chemical). ATP produced during the light reactions of photosynthesis is used specifically for the Calvin Cycle (carbon fixation) to build sugars.
14. ECM Components and Roles (2025, Q1a)
Question: Match structures to descriptions of the animal extracellular matrix.
Thorough Answer:
Structure that traps water: Proteoglycans (Letter Z), which contain many carbohydrate chains that hydration helps keep tissues plump.
Structure that resists tension: Collagen (Letter Y), the most abundant glycoprotein in the ECM.
Structure connecting ECM to cytoskeleton: Integrins (Letter W/X), which span the plasma membrane to provide a physical link.
15. ECM Protein Path (2022, Q1b / 2025, Q1b)
Question: Where are ECM proteins synthesized and how are they moved and released?

Thorough Answer: ECM proteins are synthesized in the Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (rER). They are transported to the Golgi, packaged into vesicles that move along microtubule tracks using motor proteins, and are finally released via constitutive exocytosis.
16. Nucleus Structural Terms (2025, Q2h-j)
Question: Identify the structures surrounding and within the nucleus.
Thorough Answer:

The nuclear envelope surrounds the nucleus. During cell division, 300-nm fibres coil to form metaphase chromosomes. Areas of the nucleus containing genes not currently used by the cell are called heterochromatin.
17. Factors of Continuous Variation (2024, Q5a / 2025, Q5a)
Question: Besides genetics, what factor explains the continuous range of colour variation in a species?
Thorough Answer: Environmental factors contribute to the continuous variation of phenotypes alongside genetic variation [Lecture 1 Revision, 64, 65, 82].
18. Secondary Cell Wall Characteristics (Lecture 8 Summary)
Question: When is the secondary cell wall produced and what is its unique component?

Thorough Answer: The secondary plant cell wall is produced only after cell growth has stopped. It contains the complex polymer lignin, which provides extreme structural rigidity and excludes water, making it vital for water-transporting xylem cells.
19. The Structure of the Nuclear Envelope (2021, Q1-ii / 2023, Q2d)
Question: Name the structure lining the inner envelope and its composition.
Thorough Answer: The nuclear lamina lines the inner surface of the nuclear envelope; it is composed of intermediate filaments (specifically lamins) that maintain the nucleus's shape.
20. Photosynthesis in the Dark (2023, Q2b)
Question: Explain the effect of light absence on the photosynthetic proton gradient and ATP.

Thorough Answer: Without light, the light reactions stop, meaning no electrons flow through the transport chain. Consequently, the proton gradient in the thylakoid space dissipates, and ATP production via ATP synthase ceases.

This module sets up the cell as the basic unit of life. It links evolution and the tree of life to cell architecture, macromolecules, membranes, endomembrane trafficking, cytoskeleton, energy conversion, and the nucleus.
Lecture map

items: Lecture 1: introduces life, natural selection, the tree of life, the three domains, and endosymbiosis.
Lectures 2-5: build cell structure from macromolecules, membranes, organelles, vesicle trafficking, cytoskeleton, junctions, and extracellular matrix.
Lectures 6-7: compare cellular respiration and photosynthesis as energy conversion systems built around electron transport and ATP synthase.
Lectures 8-9: consolidate eukaryotic cell organisation, the nucleus, chromatin, nuclear transport, and information storage.

blocks.text: How to use these notes

Revise this module by pairing each structure with its job. If you can explain what the structure is made of, where it sits in the cell, and what process fails when it is removed, most short-answer questions become much more predictable.
Lecture 1
Lecture Objectives
After revising this lecture, you should be able to:

Outline the characteristics that define life. Outline the scale of life. Outline the requirements of natural selection in shaping life. Outline the tree of life, how we know what it looks like, and key features including endosymbiosis. Outline what a phylogenetic tree represents. List the three domains of life.
1. Course Introduction & Administration
Academic Oversight: The CELS191 course is overseen by Professor Sally McCormick (Department of Biochemistry), whose research focus is on lipid metabolism and heart disease risk genes.
Course Coordination: Samantha Campbell is the Course Administrator, based in Mellor Laboratories (MEG04).
Modules: The course is divided into four modules: 1) Cell Structure & Diversity, 2) Molecular Biology & Genetics, 3) Human Molecular Genetics, and 4) Microbiology.

Career Pathways: The course provides a foundation for Professional Health Programs (Medicine, Pharmacy, Physiotherapy, etc.) and various Science pathways (Biochemistry, Genetics, Agriculture, Forensics, etc.).
Expectations: Students are expected to attend lectures in person and in their allocated timetable stream. Lectures are recorded and available on Blackboard for two weeks for revision.
The "Core Slide" Banner: Slides marked with this banner contain content that is directly examinable.
2. Defining Life and Its Characteristics

Definition: Life distinguishes physical entities with biological processes (like signalling and self-sustaining processes) from those that are dead or inanimate. Defining life can be ambiguous regarding viruses and synthetic life.
Key Characteristics of Life:
Cellular organization
Reproduction
Metabolism
Homeostasis
Heredity (Inheritance)
Response to stimuli Growth and development Adaptation through evolution
3. Evolution and Natural Selection
The Concept: Evolution is the process that led from tiny fossil cells to today's complex biosphere.

Natural Selection: Proposed by Charles Darwin as a testable mechanism for evolution. It acts not just on physical shape or colour, but also on biological molecules and the DNA that codes for life's functions.
Four Requirements for Natural Selection:
Variation: Individuals in a population must vary.
Inheritance: Traits must be passed genetically from parents to offspring.
Selection: Some variants must reproduce more successfully than others.
Time: Successful variations must accumulate over many generations.
4. The Tree of Life and Phylogenetics
Phylogenetic Trees: These represent family trees of organisms built by identifying shared characters, which can be physical traits or molecular sequences (like DNA).
The Three Domains: All known life is categorized into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya.

LUCA (Last Universal Common Ancestor): The common ancestor of all life on Earth, estimated to have lived 4.0 to 4.3 billion years ago. LUCA's biology can be reconstructed by identifying traits shared by all current life forms.
Domain Comparisons:
Eukarya: Possess a nuclear envelope and membrane-enclosed organelles.
Bacteria/Archaea: Lack a nuclear envelope and membrane-enclosed organelles.
Bacteria: Specifically contain peptidoglycan in their cell walls and have circular chromosomes.
5. Endosymbiosis
Theory: States that key organelles in eukaryotic cells originated from bacteria that were engulfed and "tamed" by ancestral eukaryotes.
Mitochondria: Derived from proteobacteria.
Chloroplasts: Derived from cyanobacteria.
Sequence: This engulfing process happened twice: first for mitochondria and later for chloroplasts.
Endosymbiosis in full:

The Endosymbiosis theory provides a fundamental explanation for the origin of complex eukaryotic life, suggesting that key organelles within these cells originated as independent bacteria that were engulfed and "tamed" by ancestral hosts. This transformative process occurred in distinct stages, leading to the development of the diverse range of aerobic and photosynthetic organisms seen today. The initial step toward eukaryotic complexity involved a structural transformation of an ancestral prokaryote. Scientists believe that the plasma membrane of this early cell began to infold, a process that eventually led to the formation of the nuclear envelope and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). By compartmentalizing the cell's DNA within a membrane-enclosed nucleus, the cell gained a dedicated control centre, distinguishing it from simpler prokaryotic ancestors. This internal membrane system, which includes the ER and the nuclear envelope, remains interconnected today, facilitating the synthesis and transport of proteins. Once this early eukaryotic framework was established, a significant evolutionary event occurred: the first instance of endosymbiosis. An ancestral eukaryote engulfed an aerobic bacterium, specifically a proteobacterium, but rather than digesting it, the host cell entered into a symbiotic relationship with it. Over time, these bacteria were "tamed" and evolved into mitochondria. These organelles became the primary site of cellular respiration, converting chemical energy from nutrients into ATP, which powers the cell's essential functions. This resulted in the formation of an ancestral aerobic eukaryote, a heterotroph that relied on external organic molecules for energy. Following the establishment of mitochondria, a second endosymbiotic event occurred in a lineage of these aerobic eukaryotes. These cells engulfed an additional type of bacteria-a photosynthetic bacterium known as a cyanobacterium. Just as the proteobacteria became mitochondria, these cyanobacteria were integrated into the cell and evolved into plastids, most notably chloroplasts. The inclusion of chloroplasts allowed these cells to capture light energy and convert it into chemical energy through photosynthesis. This pivotal event led to the creation of the ancestral photosynthetic eukaryote, the precursor to all modern land plants and algae. Compelling evidence for this theory exists within the organelles themselves. Both mitochondria and chloroplasts possess their own DNA and ribosomes, which are distinct from the nuclear DNA of the host cell. Furthermore, both organelles are bounded by multiple membranes; while mitochondria have two, chloroplasts feature an even more complex three-membrane system. These characteristics strongly support the conclusion that these vital components of the eukaryotic cell began as independent, living organisms.
Lecture 2
Lecture Objective

Outline the relationship between molecular ‘building blocks’ and higher-order structures in cells. Identify the structures of major types of macromolecules in cells. Describe the roles of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids in cells.
1. Composition and Scale of the Cell

Chemical Composition: A typical mammalian cell is approximately 70% water. The remaining mass consists of proteins (18%), lipids (5%), polysaccharides (2%), RNA (1.1%), and DNA (0.25%), along with inorganic ions and small metabolites.
Hierarchy of Structure: Cells are organised in a bottom-up hierarchy:
Building Blocks: Amino acids, nucleobases, simple carbohydrates, glycerol, fatty acids, and hydrocarbon rings.
Macromolecules: Proteins, DNA/RNA (nucleic acids), complex carbohydrates, and lipids.
Supramolecular Assemblies: Membranes, ribosomes, and chromatin.
Organelles: Nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi, and Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER).

Biological Scale: Biological structures range from atoms (0.1 nm) and small molecules to proteins (~10 nm), viruses (100 nm), organelles like mitochondria and nuclei (1-10 µm), and whole cells (10-100 µm).
2. Understanding Macromolecules
Definition: Organic biological molecules necessary for life, typically composed of thousands of atoms with a large molecular mass.
Building Blocks (Monomers): These are joined by chemically strong covalent bonds.
Polymeric vs. Non-polymeric:
Polymeric: Polysaccharides, nucleic acids, and proteins are created by the polymerisation of structurally similar or identical building blocks.
Non-polymeric: Lipids are considered macromolecules but do not form polymers.
3. Carbohydrates
Levels of Complexity: Categorised into monosaccharides, disaccharides, oligosaccharides (3-10 units), and polysaccharides (>10 units).
Monosaccharides: The single-unit building blocks.
Hexoses (e.g., Glucose, Fructose, Galactose) are building blocks for higher-order carbohydrates. Pentoses (e.g., Deoxyribose, Ribose) are usually parts of larger molecules like nucleic acids.
Disaccharides: Formed by two monosaccharides (e.g., Sucrose = Glucose + Fructose; Lactose = Galactose + Glucose).
Polysaccharides: Long chains used for:
Energy Storage: Starch in plants (amylose and amylopectin) and glycogen in animals.
Structure: Cellulose (fibre) is a major structural component of plant cell walls.
Recognition: Carbohydrates on the cell surface help in cell-cell recognition and can be targets for toxins and viruses.
4. Nucleic Acids
Informational Molecules: Consist of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid).
Building Block: The nucleotide, which consists of a phosphate group, a sugar (ribose or deoxyribose), and a nitrogenous base.
Bases:
Purines: Adenine (A) and Guanine (G).
Pyrimidines: Cytosine (C), Thymine (T - DNA only), and Uracil (U - RNA only).

Structure: Nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester bridges to form polynucleotide strands. DNA usually exists as a double-stranded molecule (dsDNA), while RNA is typically a single-stranded molecule (ssRNA) with a specific 3D shape.
5. Proteins
The Cell's Workhorses: Proteins perform the vast majority of biological functions.
Building Block: Polymers of amino acids. There are 20 different amino acids, each distinguished by a unique 'R' group (side chain).
Synthesis: Information flows from genes (DNA) via transcription to mRNA, which is then translated by ribosomes into a protein.
Diverse Functions: Includes structural (collagen), regulatory (insulin), contractile (actin/myosin), transport (haemoglobin), protective (antibodies), and catalytic (enzymes).
6. Lipids
Characteristics: Non-polymeric, heterogeneous, and hydrophobic (water-fearing).
Types: Triacylglycerols (fats), steroids (sterols), phospholipids, glycolipids, and fat-soluble vitamins.
Functions:
Structural: Phospholipids and cholesterol are essential components of the cell membrane. Phospholipids have a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic fatty acid tails.
Regulatory: Steroids like cholesterol serve as precursors for hormones such as testosterone and estradiol.
Energy: Triacylglycerols (TAG) are used for high-density energy storage.
Lecture 3
Lecture Objective

Describe the structure of the plasma membrane and outline its importance to cell function. Outline the role of membrane proteins. Outline mechanisms by which substances cross the plasma membrane, specifically passive transport, active transport, and co-transport. Outline the importance of organelles and sub-cellular compartments. Identify some of the key organelles in eukaryotic cells.
1. Introduction to Cell Function
Lecturer: Dr Rebecca Bird from the Department of Anatomy.
Essential Cell Tasks: To stay alive, a cell must manufacture materials, obtain raw materials from the environment, remove waste, generate energy (ATP), and maintain control over all these processes.
The Boundary: Every cell is separated from the "not alive" outside world by a plasma membrane, which provides special internal conditions and acts as a semi-permeable barrier.

Cell Size Constraints: The plasma membrane's role in exchanging oxygen, nutrients, and waste limits how large a cell can grow. Small cells are more efficient because they have a greater surface-to-volume ratio than larger cells.
2. Structure of the Plasma Membrane

The Phospholipid Bilayer: The membrane is a double layer of phospholipids. Each phospholipid has a hydrophilic phosphate head (facing the water inside/outside the cell) and hydrophobic fatty acid tails (facing inward, away from water).
Membrane Fluidity: The membrane is dynamic, not static.
Saturation: Saturated fatty acid tails pack tightly, making the membrane more viscous (less fluid); unsaturated tails have "kinks" that prevent tight packing, increasing fluidity.
Temperature: High temperatures increase fluidity, while low temperatures decrease it.
Cholesterol: In animal cells, cholesterol acts as a buffer; it reduces fluidity at moderate temperatures but hinders solidification at low temperatures by disrupting tail packing.
3. Membrane Proteins and Their Functions Proteins are embedded in the bilayer and determine most of the membrane's specific functions. Key roles include:
Signal Transduction: Relay messages from the external environment into the cell to trigger actions like growth or division.
Cell Recognition: Often involves glycoproteins (proteins with carbohydrate tags) that identify the cell to others.
Intercellular Joining: Forming long-lasting connections between adjacent cells.
Linking Cytoskeleton and ECM: Physically connecting internal microfilaments to the Extracellular Matrix (ECM) structure outside.
Membrane Transport: Controlling the movement of specific substances in and out of the cell.
4. Movement Across Membranes The mechanism used depends on the molecule's size, charge, and concentration gradient.
Passive Transport (No Energy Needed):
Diffusion: Hydrophobic/lipid-soluble molecules (like steroid hormones and gases) move directly through the membrane down their concentration gradient.
Facilitated Diffusion: Hydrophilic molecules use channels (tunnels) or carriers (which change shape) to cross the membrane down their gradient.
Osmosis: The diffusion of water through specific channels called aquaporins. Water moves from high water concentration (low solute) to low water concentration (high solute).
Active Transport (Energy Required):

Requires carrier proteins and ATP to move substances against their concentration gradient. This allows a cell to maintain internal concentrations different from its surroundings, such as the sodium-potassium pump.

Co-transport (Indirect Active Transport): One substance is pumped across the membrane using ATP; the resulting concentration gradient then powers the movement of a second substance against its own gradient.
5. Organelles and Compartmentalisation

Why Compartmentalise? Eukaryotic cells use membrane-bound organelles to create specialized environments for different processes. This keeps incompatible reactions apart, concentrates specific substances, and forms gradients.
Common Eukaryotic Organelles: Both animal and plant cells share a nucleus (double-membraned), Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER), Golgi apparatus, and mitochondria (double-membraned).
Cell-Specific Organelles:
Animal Cells: Contain lysosomes (digestive compartments).
Plant Cells: Contain chloroplasts (for photosynthesis), a large central vacuole (for water storage and pressure), and a cell wall.
Lecture 4
Lecture Objective

Define what is meant by the endomembrane system. Describe the function of the components of the endomembrane system. Outline the bulk transport processes of endocytosis (phagocytosis, pinocytosis, receptor-mediated endocytosis) and exocytosis (constitutive and regulated). Outline the role of the lysosome.
1. Introduction to Bulk Transport
Lecturer: Dr Rebecca Bird, Department of Anatomy.
The Problem: While small molecules move via membrane transport (passive or active), the cell requires mechanisms for the "bulk" movement of large substances or large volumes.
Examples: A cell manufacturing proteins for release or taking in large particles.
2. The Endomembrane System
Definition: A membrane system interconnected by direct physical contact or by transfer via vesicles.
Components: Includes the nuclear envelope, endoplasmic reticulum (ER), Golgi apparatus, vesicles, lysosomes, vacuoles, and the plasma membrane.
3. The Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)
Structure: Composed of two distinct regions: Smooth ER (sER) and Rough ER (rER).
Smooth ER (sER) Functions:

Metabolism of carbohydrates. Lipid synthesis for membranes. Detoxification of drugs and poisons. Storage of calcium ions (used as cellular signals). The amount of sER in a cell is not fixed; it can increase or decrease to meet metabolic demand.
Rough ER (rER) Functions:

Appears "rough" due to attached ribosomes (complexes of RNA and protein that carry out translation). Involved in protein synthesis. Secreted and membrane-bound proteins enter the lumen (interior) of the rER to be processed.
Note: Cytoplasmic proteins are synthesized on free ribosomes in the cytosol.
4. The Golgi Complex
Structure: A series of membrane sacs and associated vesicles with distinct polarity.
Cis face: The receiving side where vesicles from the ER arrive.
Trans face: The shipping side where processed vesicles leave.
Functions:
Receives, modifies, sorts, and ships proteins arriving from the rER.
Glycosylation: The addition or modification of carbohydrates to proteins, which is vital for secreted or cell-surface proteins.
Sorting: Adds molecular markers (like mannose 6-phosphate for lysosomal enzymes) to direct proteins to the correct vesicles.
Directing Trafficking: Adds molecular "tags" (often short proteins) to vesicles leaving the trans face so they reach their correct targets (e.g., lysosomes or the plasma membrane).
5. Bulk Transport Across the Plasma Membrane
Exocytosis: The process of transporting material out of the cell or to the cell surface.
Constitutive exocytosis: Continuous release of materials, such as extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins.
Regulated exocytosis: Materials (like hormones or neurotransmitters) are released only in response to a specific signal.
Endocytosis: The cell takes in molecules and particulate matter.
Phagocytosis: Cell "eating"; uptake of food particles into a vacuole that fuses with a lysosome for digestion. In humans, this is common in macrophages.
Pinocytosis: Cell "drinking"; non-selective uptake of extracellular fluid and solutes via vesicles formed with coat proteins.

Receptor-mediated Endocytosis: A specialized, selective form of pinocytosis using receptor proteins to capture specific bulk quantities of substances, even if they are in low concentration outside the cell.
6. Lysosomes and Vacuoles
Lysosomes: Membrane-bound organelles made by the rER and Golgi containing hydrolytic enzymes.
The interior is acidic, which is necessary for enzyme activity. They degrade proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, and nucleic acids.
Autophagy: The process of digesting and recycling the cell's own unwanted or damaged materials.
Vacuoles: Large vesicles derived from the ER and Golgi.
Food vacuoles are formed during phagocytosis.
Plant Vacuoles: Large central vacuoles absorb water, allowing plant growth and providing osmotic pressure (turgidity) to support the cell.
Lecture 5
Lecture Objective

Identify the major components of the cytoskeleton (microtubules, microfilaments, and intermediate filaments). Explain how these structures regulate cell shape. Outline the importance of cell junctions (tight, gap, and desmosomes). Describe the composition and origin of the extracellular matrix (ECM).
1. The Cytoskeleton: Structure and Dynamics

Overview: The cytoskeleton is a highly dynamic network of fibers extending throughout the cytoplasm. It provides mechanical support, maintains cell shape, and anchors or moves organelles. Unlike a bony skeleton, it can rapidly disassemble and reassemble to allow for changes in cell shape.
Three Main Components:

Microtubules (Tubulin Polymers): Hollow tubes (~25 nm) made of tubulin dimers. They resist compression and maintain cell shape. They serve as "tracks" for motor proteins to transport organelles and are essential for cell motility via cilia (rowing motion) and flagella (snake-like motion).

Microfilaments (Actin Filaments): Two intertwined strands of actin (~7 nm). They resist tension. A "cortical network" of microfilaments under the plasma membrane makes that region less fluid and helps maintain shape. They are involved in muscle contraction (via actin-myosin interactions), amoeboid movement, and cytoplasmic streaming.

Intermediate Filaments: Fibrous proteins supercoiled into thick cables (~8-12 nm). They are made of various proteins including keratins (hair/skin), lamins (nucleus), and neurofilaments (neurons). They are less dynamic and form relatively permanent structures that anchor the nucleus and other organelles.
2. How Are Cells Joined Together? (Cell Junctions)
Tight Junctions: Neighboring cells are pressed tightly together, often forming a continuous seal. Their primary function is to prevent the movement of fluid across cell layers.

Desmosomes (Anchoring Junctions): These act like "rivets" to fasten cells together into strong sheets (e.g., in muscle). They are physically connected into the cell by intermediate filaments. A "torn muscle" is effectively a series of torn desmosomes.
Gap Junctions (Communicating Junctions): These provide cytoplasmic channels between adjacent cells. Ions and small molecules pass through them, allowing for rapid intercellular communication.
3. The Extracellular Matrix (ECM)
Origin: The ECM is the non-cellular part of tissues. It is composed of materials (mostly glycoproteins) secreted by the cells themselves via the process of constitutive exocytosis.
Composition:
Collagen: The most abundant ECM glycoprotein, providing strength and resilience.
Elastin: Provides "stretch" to the tissue.
Proteoglycans: Includes molecules like hyaluronic acid, which traps water to "plump" the skin.
Fibronectins: Glycoproteins that attach the cell to the ECM.
Connection to the Cell: Membrane proteins called integrins physically connect the ECM to the internal cytoskeleton. This provides a communication link between the cell’s exterior and interior.
Lecture 6
Lecture Objective

Identify the major energy requirements of plant and animal cells. Describe the basic structure and function of the mitochondrion. Describe the importance of cellular compartments in energy conversion. Outline the mechanism of ATP synthesis and the role played by ATP in powering cellular activity.
1. Energy Flow: Respiration vs. Photosynthesis
Photosynthesis: Occurs in plants only, within chloroplasts. It uses light energy, CO2, and H2O to generate organic molecules (glucose) and O2.
Cellular Respiration: Occurs in both plants and animals within mitochondria. It breaks down organic molecules (like glucose) to generate ATP and heat energy.
Interdependence: The products of photosynthesis (O2 and organic molecules) are the reactants for respiration, while the waste products of respiration (CO2 and H2O) are used in photosynthesis.
2. Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP)
Structure: Composed of an adenine nitrogenous base, a ribose sugar, and a triphosphate group (three phosphate groups).
Function: ATP is the primary energy carrier of the cell. It allows for the controlled release of energy.

ATP Cycle: The cell continuously uses and regenerates ATP. Energy from catabolism (exergonic, energy-releasing processes) is used to combine ADP and an inorganic phosphate (Pi) into ATP. Hydrolysis of ATP then releases energy for cellular work (endergonic, energy-consuming processes).
3. Major Energy Requirements of the Cell Cells require energy for four primary tasks:
Mechanical work: For example, the movement of motor proteins along cytoskeletal tracks to move vesicles.
Making new materials: Synthesising molecules for growth and replacement.
Transport: Moving molecules across membranes against concentration gradients.
Maintaining order: Ensuring the cell remains organised and functional.
4. The Mitochondrion: Structure and Site of Respiration
Overview: Mitochondria convert chemical energy through the equation: C6H12O6 + 6O2 6CO2 + 6H2O + Energy
Quantity: There can be 1 to 1000s per cell, depending on the cell's energy demand.
Key Features: Contains its own mitochondrial DNA and ribosomes, allowing it to produce some of its own proteins.
Membrane Structure:
Outer Membrane: Encloses the organelle.
Inner Membrane: Highly folded into cristae to increase surface area; contains enzymes for oxidative phosphorylation.
Functional Compartments:
Matrix: The internal space containing enzymes for the second stage of respiration.
Intermembrane Space: The narrow region between the inner and outer membranes; essential for establishing a proton gradient.
5. The Three Stages of Cellular Respiration
Stage 1: Glycolysis
Location: Occurs in the cytosol.
Process: Glucose (6-carbon) is converted into two pyruvate (3-carbon) molecules.
Outputs: Generates 2 ATP (via substrate-level phosphorylation) and transfers electrons to NAD+ to make NADH.
Stage 2: Pyruvate Oxidation & The Citric Acid Cycle
Location: Occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.
Process: Pyruvate is converted to Acetyl CoA, which enters the cycle. CO2 is released as a waste product.
Outputs: Generates ATP and high-energy electron carriers NADH and FADH2.
Stage 3: Oxidative Phosphorylation
Location: Occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Part 1 - Electron Transport Chain (ETC): NADH and FADH2 shuttle high-energy electrons to protein complexes in the membrane. As electrons move through these complexes, protons (H+) are pumped from the matrix into the intermembrane space.

Part 2 - Chemiosmosis: A proton gradient is established (higher concentration in the intermembrane space). Protons flow back into the matrix through a protein complex called ATP synthase. This flow drives the production of ATP from ADP and Pi
Lecture 7
Lecture Objective

Describe the structure and function of the chloroplast. Outline how cells capture light energy and transduce it to cellular energy in the two stages of photosynthesis. Outline the main inputs and outputs of photosynthesis. Outline the process of energy supply in both plant and animal cells. Outline the origin of chloroplasts and mitochondria through endosymbiosis.
1. Introduction to Photosynthesis
Lecturer: Associate Professor Tina Summerfield, Department of Botany.
Role of Light: Life on Earth depends fundamentally on energy from the sun.
Energy Molecule: The primary energy-carrying molecule in cells is ATP.
The Process: Photosynthesis is the main process that generates the starting molecules (glucose) required to make ATP.
Overall Reaction: 6CO2 + 6 H2O C6H12O6 + 6O2
2. Chloroplast Structure
Size: Approximately 1-10 µm.
Genetics: Like mitochondria, chloroplasts contain their own DNA and ribosomes, allowing them to produce some of their own proteins.
Three Membranes:
Outer Membrane: Encloses the organelle.
Inner Membrane: Located just inside the outer membrane.
Thylakoid Membrane: A functionally vital internal membrane system where the light reactions occur.
Three Compartments:
Intermembrane Space: Between the inner and outer membranes.
Stroma: The fluid-filled central space where carbon fixation (Calvin Cycle) occurs.
Thylakoid Space: The space inside the thylakoids where protons (H+) accumulate.
3. The Light Reactions
Location: Occurs on the thylakoid membrane.
Mechanism: Light energy is captured by protein complexes called Photosystems (I and II), which contain chlorophyll.
Electron Flow:
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy. This energy excites electrons, which leave the photosystem. High-energy electrons move through the Photosynthetic Electron Transport Chain (ETC).
ATP and NADPH Production:

Water is split (2H2O 4H+ + O2), releasing Oxygen (O2) as a byproduct and protons into the thylakoid space. The ETC establishes a proton (H+) gradient (high concentration in thylakoid space, low in stroma). ATP synthase uses the flow of protons back into the stroma to generate ATP. The electrons eventually reduce NADP+ to form NADPH.
Outputs: The light reactions produce ATP, NADPH, and O2.
4. The Calvin Cycle (Carbon Fixation)
Location: Occurs in the stroma.
Function: Uses the ATP and NADPH generated in the light reactions to fix CO2 into carbohydrates.
Three Steps:
Fixation: Three CO2 molecules are combined with three 5-carbon molecules (Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate) to form six 3-carbon molecules.
Reduction: These 3-carbon molecules are converted into a high-energy type (Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate). One 3-carbon molecule leaves the cycle to eventually form glucose.
Regeneration: The remaining five 3-carbon molecules are converted back into three 5-carbon molecules, requiring ATP.
Output: A high-energy 3-carbon molecule; two of these are needed to create one molecule of glucose.
5. Energy Supply in Plants vs. Animals
Commonality: Both plants and animals break down glucose in the mitochondria via cellular respiration to generate ATP.
Difference: Animals must consume an external source of glucose, whereas plants generate their own via photosynthesis.
ATP Generation: In both photosynthesis and respiration, ATP is produced by ATP synthase using a proton gradient across a membrane.
6. Endosymbiosis Theory
Concept: This theory states that chloroplasts and mitochondria originated as independent bacteria that were engulfed and "tamed" by ancestral eukaryotic cells.
Origins: Chloroplasts are derived from cyanobacteria.
Evidence: Both organelles have multiple membranes, their own DNA, and their own ribosomes.
Lecture 8
Lecture Objective

Describe the structure and function of the primary plant cell wall and outline how it is synthesised. Outline the structure of the vacuole and its role in maintaining cell shape. Describe the structure and function of the secondary plant cell wall and plasmodesmata.
1. The Value of the Plant Cell Wall
A Massive Resource: Annual production of plant cell walls is estimated at 150-170 billion tons.
Energy Potential: The energy stored in these walls is nearly five times the global human energy use in 2022.
Sustainability: Research explores using the cell wall as a carbon-neutral energy source.
2. Plant Cell Components
The Definition: A plant cell is composed of the Cell Wall plus the Protoplast (everything inside the wall).
Key Structures: Includes the nucleus, Golgi apparatus, mitochondrion, chloroplast, and a large central vacuole.
Communication: Cells are connected by channels called plasmodesmata.
3. Primary Cell Wall Structure: Cellulose and the Matrix
Cellulose: The most abundant organic macromolecule on Earth. It is a glucose polymer that forms long, ribbon-like, highly ordered structures called microfibrils.
Two-Phase System:
Phase 1: Microfibrils: Crystalline phase consisting of cellulose.
Phase 2: Matrix: Non-crystalline phase consisting of hemicellulose (rigid side chains) and pectin (branched, negatively charged, binds water to form a gel).
The Network: These phases are integrated with a network of the protein extensin.
4. Regulation of Expansion: The Role of Extensin
Expansion Control: The "extensibility" (ability to expand) of a cell is controlled by extensin cross-linking.

Strengthening: When extensin cross-links with pectin and cellulose, it dehydrates the wall, reduces extensibility, and increases overall strength. This determines if a cell can or cannot continue to expand.
5. Synthesis of the Primary Cell Wall Synthesis is a coordinated three-step process:

Cellulose Microfibrils: Synthesised at the plasma membrane by enzyme complexes called rosettes (cellulose synthase). These rosettes move along the membrane parallel to cortical microtubules of the cytoskeleton.
Matrix Polysaccharides: Hemicellulose and pectin are synthesised in the Golgi apparatus and transported to the surface via vesicles.
Extensin: Synthesis begins in the rough ER, is modified (glycosylated) in the Golgi, and delivered via exocytosis.
6. Regulation of Cell Shape and Morphology
Morphology: The orientation of cellulose microfibrils dictates how a cell grows.
Randomly oriented: Cell expands equally in all directions (spherical).
Right angles to the long axis: Cell expands longitudinally (elongated).

Structural Support: The protoplast pushes against the wall to make the cell rigid (turgid), maintaining plant structure. Wilting occurs when water loss reduces protoplast volume, so it no longer presses against the wall.
7. Vacuoles and Turgor Pressure
Structure: Surrounded by a single, highly selective membrane.
Mechanism: Vacuoles contain high concentrations of solutes, causing water to move in via osmosis.
Turgor Pressure: This incoming water causes the protoplast to expand and push against the cell wall; the wall’s resistance limits water uptake and prevents the cell from bursting.
8. The Secondary Cell Wall
Occurrence: Not present in all plant cells; produced only after cell growth has stopped.
Structure: Thicker and stronger than the primary wall, consisting of multiple layers with microfibrils oriented in different directions for added strength.
Chemistry: Contains more cellulose, less pectin, and lignin.
Lignin: A complex polymer (second most abundant organic molecule) that provides extreme rigidity and excludes water. It is vital for water-transporting cells.
9. Plasmodesmata: Intercellular Communication
Definition: Cytoplasmic connections that enable cell-to-cell communication.
Structure: The plasma membrane is continuous between cells. A structure called a desmotubule (derived from the ER) runs through the centre.
Function: Small enough to prevent organelle movement but allows the free exchange of small molecules.
Lecture 9
Lecture Objective

Describe the basic structure and function of the nucleus. Describe the structure of the nuclear pore complex and its role in nucleo-cytoplasmic exchange. Describe the organisation of DNA within the nucleus. Outline the functional differences between euchromatin and heterochromatin.
1. Introduction to the Nucleus
Role: The nucleus acts as the cell’s control centre and the repository of inherited genetic information.
Scale: It is typically the most prominent organelle, measuring 5-10 µm in diameter.
Genetic Content: While some genes are found in mitochondria and chloroplasts, the nucleus contains the vast majority of the cell's genes.
The Workflow: Genes in the nucleus code for proteins; RNA carries this information out of the nucleus to ribosomes, which then translate it into proteins.
2. Nuclear Structure

The Nuclear Envelope: A double membrane structure (inner and outer membranes) separated by a perinuclear space. Each membrane is a phospholipid bilayer. The outer membrane is continuous with the Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER).
The Nuclear Lamina: A network of intermediate filaments (specifically lamins) that lines the inner surface of the envelope. It maintains the nucleus's shape and helps organise DNA packing.

Clinical Note: Genetic defects in lamin proteins prevent a typical nuclear lamina from forming, resulting in misshapen nuclei. This limits cell division and can lead to Progeria, a condition causing premature aging.

The Nucleolus: A prominent, non-membrane bound region within the nucleus of non-dividing cells. It is responsible for synthesising ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and assembling ribosomal subunits, which are then transported to the cytoplasm.
3. Nucleo-Cytoplasmic Exchange (Nuclear Pores)
The Nuclear Pore Complex: Channels made of proteins called nucleoporins that span the nuclear envelope. There are approximately 1,000 pores per cell.
Movement OUT of the Nucleus: mRNA (carrying gene information), tRNA, and ribosomal subunits (needed to build proteins).
Movement INTO the Nucleus: Control signals (to turn genes on/off), building blocks for RNA synthesis, and energy required for chemical synthesis.
4. DNA Organisation within the Nucleus
The Challenge: A single human cell contains about 2.5 metres of DNA, which is 250,000 times the diameter of the nucleus. It must be tightly packed yet accessible.
Levels of Packaging:
DNA Double Helix: 2 nm in diameter.
Nucleosomes: DNA wraps around histone proteins (H2-H4) to form a 10-nm fibre, often described as "beads on a string".
30-nm Fibre: Further interactions with histone H1 cause the 10-nm fibre to coil. 300-nm Fibre: The 30-nm fibre loops to form this larger structure.
Metaphase Chromosomes: During cell division, the 300-nm fibres coil even tighter into distinct chromosomes.
Interphase Organisation: Chromosomes are not randomly placed; coloured tags show they occupy specific territories, and pairs are generally not located together.
5. Chromatin Types
Euchromatin: Less tightly packed and less electron-opaque; it contains genes that are currently being used (active) by the cell.
Heterochromatin: Highly packed and more electron-opaque; it contains genes that are silent or not being used by the cell.
Dynamics: The relationship between these two forms is dynamic, changing based on the cell's needs.
Common mistakes
Lecture 1: The Diversity of Life

Origin of Organelles: A common mistake is confusing the bacterial ancestors of organelles. Mitochondria are derived specifically from proteobacteria, while chloroplasts are derived from cyanobacteria.
The Three Domains: Students often incorrectly include viruses as a domain of life. All known life is actually organised into only three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya (Eukaryotes).

Natural Selection Requirements: For evolution via natural selection to occur, four specific conditions must be met: variation, inheritance, selection, and time. Omitting any of these is a common error.
Lecture 2: Building Blocks of Cells
Polymer Classification: A major misconception is that all macromolecules are polymers. While polysaccharides, nucleic acids, and proteins are created by polymerisation, lipids are non-polymeric.

Sugar Units: Confusing hexose and pentose monosaccharides is common. Hexoses (like glucose) are building blocks for higher-order carbohydrates, whereas pentoses (like ribose and deoxyribose) are usually parts of larger molecules like nucleic acids.
Plant vs. Animal Carbohydrates: Misidentifying storage polysaccharides is frequent. Starch is the plant energy carbohydrate, while glycogen is the animal version.
Lecture 3: Plasma Membrane & Organelles

Membrane Permeability: A common mistake is thinking the phospholipid bilayer is an impermeable wall. It is actually a semi-permeable barrier; it is permeable to lipid-soluble (hydrophobic) molecules like gases and steroid hormones, but restricts water-soluble and charged molecules like glucose and ions.

Fluidity Regulation: It is often incorrectly assumed that cholesterol only makes a membrane more or less fluid. In reality, cholesterol stabilises fluidity, acting as a buffer against temperature changes.

Transport Gradients: A frequent error is confusing the direction of movement. In passive transport, molecules move down their concentration gradient (no energy), whereas in active transport, they move against it (requires energy).
Lecture 4: Endomembrane System & Bulk Transport

Organelle Flexibility: It is a mistake to think the amount of Smooth ER (sER) in a cell is fixed. The cell can increase or decrease the amount of sER to meet metabolic demands, such as detoxification needs.
Golgi Polarity: A common error is misidentifying the "shipping" and "receiving" sides of the Golgi complex. Vesicles arrive at the cis face and processed vesicles leave from the trans face.

Selectivity in Endocytosis: Students often fail to distinguish between types of bulk intake. Pinocytosis is non-selective ("cell drinking"), whereas receptor-mediated endocytosis is highly selective, using proteins to capture specific solutes.
Lectures 5-8: Cell Shape, Respiration, Photosynthesis, and Cell Walls

Energy Generation Mechanism: A common misconception is that plant and animal cells use entirely different mechanisms for ATP. In reality, both use ATP synthase powered by a proton gradient across a membrane (mitochondrial or thylakoid) [Lecture 6 & 7 Objectives, 49].

Turgor Pressure: A mistake is assuming the cell wall alone provides structure. Plant structural support requires turgor pressure, where the protoplast pushes against the wall due to water intake in the vacuole [Lecture 8 Objectives, 49].

Cell Wall Synthesis: Students often forget that the secondary cell wall is not universal; it is produced only after cell growth has stopped and contains lignin to exclude water [Lecture 8 Objectives, 49].
Lecture 9: The Nucleus

Protein Synthesis Location: A common error is thinking proteins are assembled inside the nucleus. While the nucleolus makes ribosomal subunits and rRNA, these must be transported to the cytoplasm for final assembly into functional ribosomes and subsequent protein synthesis.

Chromatin States: Confusing euchromatin and heterochromatin is frequent. Euchromatin is less tightly packed and contains active genes being used by the cell, while heterochromatin is tightly packed and contains silent genes.
